memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "The city and all that is in it are to be devoted to the Lord. Only Rahab the prostitute and all who are with her in her house shall be spared, because she hid the spies we sent. But keep away from the devoted things, so that you will not bring about your own destruction by taking any of them. Otherwise you will make the camp of Israel liable to destruction and bring trouble on it. All the silver and gold and the articles of bronze and iron are sacred to the Lord and must go into his treasury." — Josh 6:17-19 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
This is a hard passage, and we should not rush past its difficulty. Jericho and everything in it was "devoted to the Lord" — set apart entirely for God, which here meant its complete destruction as an act of divine judgment. We must place this honestly in its setting: this was a specific, unrepeatable command in redemptive history. God was executing judgment on a deeply corrupt Canaanite culture, using Israel as His instrument at a particular moment. This is not a pattern for how God's people are to treat their enemies today. Under the New Covenant, Christ commands us to love our enemies and pray for them (Matt 5:44).

Yet even in this severe passage, grace shines. Rahab and her household are spared — a Canaanite family rescued by faith right in the middle of a city under judgment. The God who judges is also the God who saves all who turn to Him. Rahab's scarlet cord marked out a pocket of mercy in a city of judgment.

There is also a solemn warning: keep away from the "devoted things," or you will bring destruction on yourself. What belonged to God was not to be treated as common plunder. God's holiness was not to be taken lightly.

The deepest note here points beyond Jericho to the final reckoning of all things. God is holy and just, and sin truly is judged. But in Christ, God took that judgment upon Himself so that all who trust Him, like Rahab, might be spared. The cross is where perfect justice and saving mercy meet.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. How do you hold together God's justice and His mercy, both seen in this passage?
2. Rahab found mercy by faith amid judgment — does that deepen your gratitude for grace?
3. How does the cross help you understand a God who is both perfectly just and saving?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Holy God, You are both just and merciful. Thank You that in Christ, judgment fell on Him so that I, like Rahab, could be spared. Help me never take Your holiness lightly. Amen.
